content.text: Chapter Seventeen
Admission to the Horde
Rommath’s transit circle opened beneath a sky the color of old iron.

Falanaras crossed first with his sword on his back and felt Silvermoon vanish behind him. The spell released him onto rain-dark flagstones inside the ruins of a gatehouse. Cold entered through the joints of his armor before his sight cleared. Broken walls enclosed a receiving yard where Forsaken wardens stood around a second ring cut into the stone. Beyond them, dead trees bent across the hills of Tirisfal, and the remains of Lordaeron’s capital rose against the eastern gloom.

The Forsaken did not raise their weapons. One deathguard watched the green fel light in Falanaras’s eyes with faint curiosity, then gave the receiving circle a soldier’s inspection. No one had promised affection on either side.

Liadrin emerged behind him, followed by Lor’themar, Lethira, the remainder of the Blood Knight guard, and two Farstriders carrying the sealed terms from Windrunner Spire. Rommath came last. The portal folded shut at his back, leaving only a brief violet afterimage and the smell of charged stone.
“The return circle remains keyed for six hours,” Rommath said. “After that, Silvermoon must open it from their side.”
“Comforting,” Lethira said. “We have been granted an exact measure of time in which diplomacy may fail.”

Serenya Duskrunner stepped from the ruined arch. She wore the same dark leathers as at the signal stone, though Undercity’s black arrowhead marked one shoulder. Four dark rangers accompanied her. Falanaras recognized two from southern Eversong. Their presence eased nothing in Liadrin’s posture, but the honor guard received them as known soldiers.
Serenya gave Lor’themar a shallow bow. “The banshee queen waits below. The Horde representatives have begun arriving.”
“We will not keep them waiting,” Lor’themar said.

They left the gatehouse under escort. The road crossed a city that had died in stages. Outer houses had collapsed behind weeds and blackened hedges. The inner wall still bore the royal crest beneath Scourge cuts deep enough to catch rain. Forsaken sentries occupied the surviving towers with a practical indifference to the human dead whose kingdom had raised them.

Falanaras had seen human banners above camps in the southern kingdoms and human dead marching beneath Arthas. He had never entered Lordaeron while it lived. The ruin nevertheless felt familiar. A capital abandoned after slaughter required little translation. Silvermoon had hidden more of its wound behind crimson cloth and restored crystal, but the same absence waited wherever a doorway still expected a household that would never return.

The broken royal courtyard opened ahead. Dead rose petals clung to seams in the paving despite the rain. A dark stain led through the doors of the throne room, too old to remain blood and too deliberate to be mistaken for weathering. No one in the delegation asked who had died along that path.
Lethira slowed beneath the throne-room arch. Serenya matched her pace.
“Arthas walked here after he killed his father,” Serenya said. Her voice held no reverence for the memory. “The echoes repeat it when the upper halls are quiet.”
Lethira’s gaze followed the stain. “Does your queen ever come this way?”
“When she chooses.” Serenya’s eyes remained forward. “She does not yield ground because it remembers him.”

The passage beyond the throne room descended toward a bank of iron lifts. Chains rattled in shafts wide enough to swallow a siege tower. The delegation entered one platform with their escort. Serenya pulled a lever, and the living capital rose away above them.

Cold air climbed from below carrying alchemical bitterness, rot, wet stone, and the sour reek of green channels moving through buried streets. One of the younger Blood Knights swallowed hard. Liadrin did not look at him. Falanaras kept his breathing even and watched rings of masonry pass the open cage: crypts, old sewers, Scourge-cut tunnels, then arches strengthened with Forsaken iron.

The lift released them into a city built for inhabitants who did not breathe. Poisonous water shone beneath bridges. Apothecaries passed with stoppered crates while deathguards drilled beside old tombs. Orcs, trolls, and tauren moved through the Trade Quarter among the Forsaken, visibly uncomfortable and entirely unsurprised. The sight carried its own argument. The Horde already contained peoples who found one another difficult to endure.

An orc quartermaster stopped counting spearheads as the sin’dorei passed. His eyes settled on the green light in Falanaras’s face, then shifted to the gold beneath Liadrin’s green eyes. He touched two fingers to his own green skin above the gorget, acknowledging the resemblance.

Falanaras understood the accusation before the orc spoke it. Their bodies both carried the history of power accepted in desperation. The orcs had at least learned where their road ended. Silvermoon was still naming its first milestones.
Sylvanas received them in the Royal Quarter beneath banners bearing the broken mask of the Forsaken.

At Windrunner Spire she had stood inside the remains of a life taken from her. Here every arch answered to the rule she had built afterward. Deathguards lined the chamber. Dark rangers watched from shadowed galleries. Apothecaries waited near a side door with ink, seals, and instruments whose medicinal purpose was not obvious. Sylvanas sat beneath a stone canopy in dark armor, one hand resting against the arm of her throne.
A dreadlord stood behind her.

Varimathras towered over the Forsaken court with folded wings and a courtier’s stillness that could not disguise the weight of him. His hide held the bruised color of storm clouds. Curved horns framed a face made for contempt. Fel heat touched Falanaras’s senses from across the chamber, heavier than the crystals sustaining Silvermoon’s wards and fouler in its intent.
Liadrin’s stolen radiance stirred. Falanaras felt the answering impulse in his own chest and held it quiet.
“Regent Lord,” Sylvanas said. “You reached my city without incident.”
“Your escort was efficient.” Lor’themar’s gaze moved once to Varimathras. “Your court remains surprising.”
The dreadlord smiled. “The living elf objects to demons while carrying their stain in his eyes.”
Rommath looked him over with the clinical displeasure he reserved for defective apparatus. “I object only to pets that mistake the audience for their master.”

Varimathras’s wings opened a handspan. Fel pressure thickened the chamber. “Careful, magister. Silvermoon cages a holy creature and feeds its streets with fel. The difference between servant and master may trouble you sooner than you imagine.”
Rommath drew breath to answer. “Enough,” Sylvanas said.
The word cut through the fel pressure. Varimathras held himself rigid for one dangerous breath. Then his wings folded, the heat withdrew, and he lowered his head. Obedience cost him visibly.
Sylvanas turned her red gaze upon Rommath. “He offered me his brothers to purchase his life. He serves because I continue to find value in his survival. Draw whatever lesson seems useful.”
“Several,” Rommath said. “None flattering.”

Lor’themar presented the provisional terms. A Forsaken clerk read each clause aloud: the clearing and rebuilding of Tranquillien, paired command, agreed garrison strength, shared stores, coordinated action against the Scourge, and the preservation of Quel’Thalas’s sovereignty. Sylvanas interrupted twice to tighten language around courier access and the obligation to answer an immediate threat. Lethira corrected the field definitions. By the time the seals were pressed beneath the agreement, nothing had become warmer between them. It had become harder to misunderstand.
“The wider question remains,” Sylvanas said. “I can sponsor Silvermoon. I cannot admit it.”
“What has been said against us?” Lor’themar asked.

“That your people are starving aristocrats who discovered fel magic, enslaved a source of Holy Light, abandoned one alliance, and followed a prince who has now abandoned them.” Sylvanas’s mouth tightened. “Most accusations become persuasive when arranged well.”
Liadrin stepped forward. “You intend to place the Blood Knights before them as evidence against us.”
“As evidence,” Sylvanas replied. “What judgment follows is theirs. The Horde knows enough to fear the method. Concealment beyond that would only make cowards of us all.”
“We will answer for what we do,” Liadrin said. “We will not surrender the workings beneath Silvermoon to earn a hearing.”
Sylvanas regarded her for a moment. “A sensible limit. Keep it until Thrall decides whether it resembles prudence or evasion.”
A deathguard entered and bowed. “The Warchief has arrived.”

For the first time since the delegation entered, Sylvanas’s attention moved past the political use of the room. Her gaze caught on Lethira’s ranger clasp, worn smooth from years before the fall. The pause lasted no more than a breath.
“The Horde will judge what Quel’Thalas has become,” she said. “Give it reason to remember what your people endured to remain.”
The delegation waited in an antechamber while the council assembled.

No window interrupted the black stone. A channel of green fluid passed behind an iron grate beneath the floor, warming the room with poisonous vapor. Rommath and Lor’themar reviewed their order of argument. Liadrin stood apart with her gauntlets resting against the pommel of her sword. The other Blood Knights remained in the corridor under guard.
Lethira leaned against the wall beside Falanaras. “At the Spire, I could still see where she used to stand.”
Falanaras knew she meant Sylvanas. “You can see it here too.”

“That is the difficulty.” Lethira rubbed her thumb across the old clasp. “At Windrunner Spire, every broken stone accused Arthas. Here the stones obey her. I thought one place would show what remained and the other what replaced it.”
“And?”

“They are both her.” Lethira’s voice dropped. “The woman who counted our arrows. The thing Arthas raised. The queen who keeps a demon at heel and still notices a ranger clasp she issued before either of us had learned to distrust orders.”

Falanaras remembered the anti-Horde priest in the Walk of Elders, his voice seized by magisters and forced to praise the alliance while tears ran down his face. “Recognition does not make command safe.”
“No.” Lethira released the clasp. “It makes refusal harder.”
The council doors opened before either could answer further.
Thrall stood at the head of a long stone table scarred by weapons and chemical spills.

The Warchief was younger than the weight of his title suggested. Broad shoulders filled his black plate, and his hands rested openly on the table. Doomhammer hung across his back. The green of his skin carried no ornament or attempt at concealment. Falanaras had seen orcs only through inherited war records and the reports of scouts. He had expected savagery to announce itself. Thrall’s stillness held something more difficult: strength taught to fear its own worst use.

Cairne Bloodhoof sat at Thrall’s right, enormous even while seated. Age silvered the fur around his muzzle. Feathers and carved beads hung from his braids, and the quiet around him felt deliberate rather than empty. Vol’jin occupied the next place, narrow-eyed and watchful, one tusk catching the sick green light. Sylvanas sat opposite them with Varimathras absent from the chamber. Orc officers, Darkspear envoys, tauren elders, and Forsaken ministers filled the remaining seats.
Lor’themar remained standing. Liadrin, Rommath, Lethira, and Falanaras took places behind him.

Thrall began without ceremony. “Sylvanas Windrunner asks the Horde to admit Silvermoon and Quel’Thalas. She claims your kingdom can hold the northern road, strengthen our war against the Scourge, and answer Horde calls with soldiers and magic. Tell us why we should accept the risks she brings with you.”

Lor’themar did not offer gratitude for the hearing. “Because the risks already exist. The Scourge remain between our borders. The Amani strike every weakness they find. The Alliance has neither forgiven us nor offered protection. If Quel’Thalas falls, the force that destroys it will not stop at our southern line. Silvermoon brings territory, trained armies, intelligence from the Eastern Kingdoms, access to the northern coast, and a people with reason to keep every one of those assets from becoming an enemy’s.”
An orc commander tapped one thick finger against the table. “Your people brought fel into their homes.”
Rommath answered. “We use controlled sources to sustain wards, industry, and a population severed from the Sunwell. We do not drink demon blood. We do not surrender command to demons.”
“You think control makes corruption obedient?” the commander asked.
“I think knowledge makes power governable,” Rommath said. “Your history may argue otherwise. Ours has not granted us the luxury of refusing every dangerous tool.”

Thrall’s gaze hardened. “Our history argues because we buried clans beneath it. Orcs accepted power that promised victory. It marked our skin before it consumed our will, and many called the change strength until they could no longer remember what strength had been for.”
His eyes moved over the blood elves’ green-lit faces. The resemblance was imperfect. It remained close enough to wound.
“We did not come to ask you to admire our methods,” Lor’themar said. “We came because isolation is killing us more reliably than pride can save us.”

Lor’themar continued before another question could come. “There remains the matter of the Amani. They joined the old Horde in burning our forests and still seek our destruction. Silvermoon will not enter any alliance that asks us to forget Zul’jin’s claim upon Quel’Thalas.”
Vol’jin’s fingers tightened around his staff. “Who be askin’ you to forget? You speak of da Amani and look to me. You think tusks make one tribe answer for another?”
“I think an old war will enter this alliance whether either of us invites it,” Lor’themar said.

“Den learn who stands before you. Darkspear blood be troll blood, but it do not belong to Zul’jin. Da Amani chose their war. My tribe chose dis Horde, and we bled beside peoples our ancestors never knew. If Silvermoon joins us, you name your enemies true. You do not spit ‘troll’ and make every tribe carry da Amani’s crimes. Bring that pride into dis Horde, and it poison every line we try to hold.”
Lethira spoke from behind Lor’themar. “Amani arrows have pointed north all my life. I have no cause to place a Darkspear spear beside them unless its wielder does.”
Vol’jin looked at her ranger bow. “You seen a Darkspear spear hold your line?”
“Not yet,” Lethira said. “I have seen Forsaken arrows do it. I can judge the next soldier by where they stand.”
“Dat be a beginning,” Vol’jin said. “Keep your pride from poisoning it.”
Cairne’s deep voice entered the chamber without force. “There is another power to discuss.”
Liadrin met his gaze.
“A captive being of Light suffers so your warriors may heal and kill.” Cairne’s grief held no theatrical outrage. “You carry that suffering across distance and call upon it by choice.”
“Yes,” Liadrin said.
“Do you believe need makes the suffering just?”

“I believe need makes refusal a choice with victims of its own.” Liadrin kept both hands visible. “Our order saved defenders who would have died in southern Eversong. We broke Scourge workings our diminished magisters could not have broken in time. None of that dulls our captive's pain. None of it grants us innocence.”
Cairne studied her. “Then what governs you?”
“Training. Command. Witness. We name misuse as failure even when it wins.”
“Your order writes the law, wields the power, and judges the breach.”
Liadrin’s jaw tightened. “Yes.”
The answer settled more heavily than a defense would have. Cairne inclined his head, acknowledging honesty without accepting the act.

Sylvanas placed one hand on the table. “The Horde did not require the Forsaken to become pleasant before accepting our soldiers, roads, and war against the Scourge. Silvermoon offers the same practical proof. Its knights held a breached boundary beside my rangers. Its regent has accepted terms at Tranquillien that place blood elf and Forsaken troops under mutual goals. If moral purity is the price of admission, empty the chamber before you begin with them.”
“You advocate loudly for a living kingdom,” an orc elder said.
Sylvanas’s red eyes found him. “I advocate for a northern ally that keeps the Scourge away from Forsaken territory. My reasons do not require your romance.”
The rebuke concealed more than it denied. Falanaras saw Lethira hear it too.
Thrall looked from Liadrin to Falanaras. “At Windrunner Spire, one of your knights offered to be tested under pressure.”
Falanaras stepped forward. “I did.”
“A demonstration in a hall proves that the power answers,” Thrall said. “It does not prove that your order can fight with honor, and be fit to stand beside Horde soldiers.”
“Then choose the test.”
A low voice came from among the orc officers. “I will test him.”

Gorath Stonebinder rose. He wore layered mail beneath hides marked with ocher and ash. His black hair had been bound behind his head, and carved stones hung from his belt beside a one-handed axe. Rain-dark green skin showed at his throat and across his broad hands. The power around him moved through the floor and the moisture in the walls, quiet until acknowledged.
“Your eyes carry fel,” Gorath said. “Your hands carry stolen Light. Your people call both power. I want to see what that word means when power answers back.”
“Then watch,” Falanaras said.
Gorath’s tusks showed around something that was not a smile. “We will hear.”
They returned to the ruined courtyard above Undercity under a hard afternoon rain.

Forsaken guards cleared the broken flagstones while the council gathered beneath the surviving arcade. Thrall and Cairne stood at its center. Vol’jin watched from beside a cracked pillar. Sylvanas remained in the open rain with her hood drawn low, occupying Lordaeron’s ruin as if weather had lost authority over her.
Liadrin fastened Falanaras’s final shoulder clasp. “They expect power.”
“Gorath will have it.”
“Give them no reason to mistake discipline for timidity.” Her fingers tightened once against the plate. “Fight as a Blood Knight. Win with honor.”

Falanaras drew his two-handed sword. He had left the spellbreaker glaive behind when he entered Liadrin’s order, but its lessons remained in his hands: read the hostile current, find where intent passed into power, break the use, subdue the source.
Across the courtyard, Gorath pressed his palm to the wet stone. “No killing stroke,” he said. “Yield ends the fight. Losing the weapon does not.”
“Agreed.”
Thrall lifted one hand. “Begin.”
The courtyard struck first.

Stone rose beneath Falanaras’s forward foot. He shifted before the slab could lock his knee, but a second ridge caught his heel and threw him sideways. Wind hit while he recovered, driving rain through his vision and turning the sword’s broad blade into a sail. Gorath crossed the distance behind it with his axe held low.

Falanaras caught the axe on his crossguard. The impact jolted both arms. Gorath drove a shoulder into his breastplate and released another pulse through the ground. Flagstones bucked. Falanaras yielded three steps rather than fight the earth for ownership of his footing.

Gorath pursued. His axe moved in short practical cuts, forcing the longer sword to work inside its preferred reach. Falanaras turned one blow, caught another against his vambrace, and felt the edge score black lacquer from the plate. He answered with the pommel. Gorath slipped it and swept his free hand upward.
Lightning flashed from palm to sword.

The lightning entered through sword and gauntlets. Wards etched into Falanaras’s plate resisted the current’s attempt to seize muscle and nerve; they divided enough of it across his armor to keep his heart beating, not enough to spare him pain. White fire crossed his sight. He broke contact by falling backward, rolled through mud, and came up with one knee refusing to straighten. Scorched leather smoked around both hands.
Gorath waited only long enough to see whether he could stand. Then the shaman stamped.

A line of stone teeth tore across the courtyard. Falanaras called the Light hard. M’uru’s pain entered with it, a fractured tone beneath the rain, and red-gold radiance surged along his left arm into a slanted barrier. The first stone exploded against it. He drove through the second impact, turned the ward like a shield, and smashed the third ridge aside before cutting toward Gorath’s shoulder.

Gorath turned the blade with his axe and sent wind between them. The blast carried no heat, yet it struck like a gate thrown open by a siege ram. Falanaras skidded across the wet stones. The shaman did not attack his strength. He attacked every place strength required stability.
Falanaras changed his grip and began reading.

Elemental magic did not lie in wards as arcane work did. It moved through relationship: Gorath’s request, the answering pressure below, the breath drawn before wind gathered, the sharp lift in the air before lightning chose metal. The spellbreaker in Falanaras could not strip command from the earth. He could still see when the command passed between them.

Gorath raised his axe. Falanaras moved before the lightning came, thrust the sword into a crack between flagstones, and released the hilt. The bolt struck the grounded blade. Thunder burst across the courtyard. Gorath had already called wind to punish the expected advance, but Falanaras went low beneath it, one palm in the mud, and used a brief flare through his legs to drive himself forward.

His shoulder struck Gorath’s waist. They fell together. The orc hammered an elbow against the back of his helm and rolled. Falanaras caught the axe haft with both hands. Gorath pulled, stronger at that angle, while stone climbed around Falanaras’s forearms in heavy bands.

The captive Light answered at once. Falanaras sent a narrow current through his limbs, loosening the stone’s hold on his movement without pretending to command the earth itself. The bands cracked away from his forearms. He carried the same release into the axe haft between them, opening Gorath’s grip without crushing the ribs beneath it.
Power without placement was waste. The spellbreaker’s lesson had survived every change of weapon: find the point that governed the contest and break it.

Falanaras tore one hand free, struck the inside of Gorath’s elbow, and ripped the axe from his grip. The orc answered with his forehead. Falanaras’s helm rang. Gorath surged upright, empty-handed and blood dripping from one tusk, while broken stone hissed around their boots.
Falanaras kicked the axe away and reached for his sword. Gorath called the earth beneath it. The weapon sank deeper into the crack as stone closed around the blade.
Losing the weapon did not end the fight.

Gorath opened both hands. Wind circled him, pulling rain into a gray veil. Lightning began to gather above the courtyard rather than in his palms. The watching orcs stepped back beneath the arcade. Thrall did not stop him.

Falanaras had no steel to ground the strike and no stable footing from which to evade it. He planted both boots and gave the stolen Light one immediate purpose: stand between his body and the descending force. M’uru’s anguish sharpened as crimson-gold radiance vaulted over him in a broad arch, its surface layered like heated plate.
Lightning fell.

The barrier caught the bolt and bent nearly to his shoulders. Light and lightning filled the courtyard with red-white glare. Falanaras could not steal the answer Gorath had received from the storm. He could choose what surface received it. At the instant the strike spread across the arch, he turned the barrier’s face and gave the current a steeper path into the flooded stones. Thunder rolled under the arcades as the grounded lightning split flagstones on both sides of him.
Steam erupted. Gorath’s wind broke apart.

Falanaras collapsed the barrier. Part of its released force gathered around his right fist, brightening toward a white core as he drove through the steam. The holy discharge reached Gorath a fraction before the gauntlet and locked the orc’s limbs in place. The physical blow struck his chest while he could not turn with it. Gorath left his feet and hit the base of a broken pillar hard enough to split its remaining plaster.
Gorath tried to rise. One knee held. The other failed. He reached toward the earth.

Falanaras retrieved the shaman’s axe and crossed the last steps. He bound red-gold radiance along its edge and held the stored force there, ready to release only if Gorath refused the end. The weapon gilded the rain without spending its charge.
Gorath’s throat lay exposed. Falanaras had sworn himself to a duel without killing. Honor demanded that he end the contest by forcing Gorath’s yield and spare the life already at his mercy.

Falanaras brought the axe down. Its burning edge stopped against the iron rim of Gorath’s breastplate, close enough that heat raised steam from the rainwater there. The force in Falanaras’s arm remained ready, visible, and entirely still.
“Yield,” he said.
Gorath looked at the burning edge, then at Falanaras’s face. Rain ran through the blood at his mouth.
Gorath released his hand from the earth. “I yield.” Only then did Falanaras dismiss the holy fire along the axe.

Falanaras stepped back and offered him the axe handle first. Gorath accepted it, rose with a grimace, and gave him a warrior’s nod. Respect had entered the space between them. Trust had not yet followed.
The council returned below while healers bound Gorath’s ribs and treated the burns beneath Falanaras’s gauntlets.

No one pretended the duel had answered Cairne’s objection. M’uru remained captive beneath Silvermoon. Fel still shone in sin’dorei eyes. Kael’thas’s betrayal remained recent enough to stain every promise made in his wake. Falanaras had proved that Blood Knight power could withstand a shaman’s full assault, answer with overwhelming force, and remain governed by skill, command, and an oath honored at the point of victory. The Horde still had to decide whether one warrior’s honor could stand as evidence for an order and a nation.
Thrall called Lor’themar forward. The Warchief stood with Cairne, Vol’jin, and Sylvanas behind the long table. Gorath had taken a place among the orc officers despite the binding around his chest.

“The Horde was formed by peoples who survived powers that expected them to disappear,” Thrall said. “Orcs carry the shame of corruption we chose. The Darkspear carry exile. The tauren remember enemies that hunted them from their homes. The Forsaken came to us feared by every living nation, and Cairne asked me to judge what they did with freedom rather than what slavery had made of them.”
Cairne’s grave expression did not change. Sylvanas watched Thrall with the patience of someone hearing her own history used for another purpose.

“Silvermoon brings dangers,” Thrall continued. “Fel has marked your people. Your prince sold loyalty for power. Your Blood Knights wield suffering as a weapon. Admission does not make those truths smaller.”
Lor’themar held his gaze. “We did not ask it to.”

“Good. Then hear the obligation. If Quel’Thalas enters the Horde, its soldiers answer Horde calls. Its roads and intelligence serve common defense. Its leaders speak in council and accept that other members will speak against them. No blood elf may treat Darkspear, tauren, or Forsaken lives as lesser payment for Silvermoon’s survival. The Horde is not a shield hired for your border.”
“Quel’Thalas accepts those obligations as a sovereign member,” Lor’themar said. “It does not enter as Sylvanas’s dependency or as conquered territory.”
“Agreed,” Thrall said. “Then by the authority entrusted to the Warchief and the consent given in this council, I admit the blood elves of Quel’Thalas into the Horde.”

No cheer followed. Orc hands struck breastplates in acknowledgment. Darkspear envoys touched fists to their chests. Cairne bowed his head. The Forsaken remained still until Sylvanas rose, and then their weapons struck the floor as one.

Liadrin exhaled beside Falanaras. The sound carried no relief. They had acquired obligations, roads, and allies. Nothing beneath Silvermoon had become less captive. Nothing in the Walk of Elders had become more freely spoken.
A courier entered before the seals had cooled. He wore Silvermoon crimson beneath a Forsaken travel cloak. Lor’themar broke the message, read it once, and passed it to Liadrin.
“More arrests?” Falanaras asked quietly.

Liadrin’s mouth tightened. “Three gatherings dispersed. Two magisters injured. A mana ration station burned in the Bazaar after someone accused its keeper of poisoning the supply for the Horde.” She lowered the letter. “Theron reports the Blood Knight patrols are holding.”

Across the chamber, orc officers were already arguing over how soon Silvermoon could provide troops in Lordaeron. A Forsaken minister named Tranquillien’s supply requirements to one of Rommath’s aides. Vol’jin spoke with Lethira about Amani movement east of the Dead Scar. Admission had become work before the declaration finished echoing.
Gorath approached with one arm held close to his ribs. “Blood Knight.”
“Stonebinder.”
“You fought with power enough to kill me,” Gorath said. His gaze moved to the bandages beneath Falanaras’s gauntlets. “You fought with honor.”
“That is our oath.”

Gorath considered the answer and nodded once. “An oath is easy in a courtyard, with witnesses and a friendly voice to call the end. I will see whether yours holds when an enemy offers no honor in return.”
Sylvanas joined Lor’themar at the council doors. “You have what you came for.”
“Membership,” Lor’themar said. “Trust appears to have been withheld.”

“Trust from the others will take time,” Sylvanas said. Her gaze drifted briefly toward the ceiling, beyond which ruined Lordaeron endured the rain. “Your people already have the trust of the Forsaken. My rangers have watched sin’dorei hold the same line, and they do not grant that judgment lightly. Let the rest learn.”

The return transit would not open for another hour. Falanaras stood among new allies beneath a dead kingdom and listened to them decide where Silvermoon’s soldiers would bleed first. The Horde had admitted the sin’dorei in law. Belonging waited beyond the next order, the next field, and the first time strangers trusted his strength beside them.
